newsitem.title: UK: Total says no deal yet on Iraqi crude exports.
newsitem.headline: Total says no deal yet on Iraqi crude exports.

text.p: French oil company Total SA said on Tuesday it had not yet finalised a contract to buy Iraqi crude oil under the terms of a United Nations oil-for-food deal which cleared its final major hurdle last week.
"We have not signed anything yet but we are proposing to lift about 30,000 barrels per day (bpd) if we agree with Iraq," said a Total spokesman by telephone from Paris.
Iraq last month accepted U.N. terms for the limited U.N. deal which allows Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months on a renewable basis.
Iraq's oil minister Amer Rasheed was quoted by a Baghdad newspaper on Tuesday as saying Iraq expected to sign oil contract with 50 international firms in the next two days.
Taha Hmud Mosa, senior under-secretary at the oil ministry in Baghdad, told Reuters the deals could be completed "in several days as the companies are ready waiting for the signal to start loading."

In 1989, the last full year before the U.N. imposed its oil embargo against Baghdad for invading neighbour Kuwait, France's Elf Aquitaine and Total were major users of Iraqi crude, together taking 115,00 bpd.
Elf would not comment on whether it had already signed a contract with Iraq's state marketer SOMO but an Elf spokesman reiterated the company's interest in lifting Iraqi crude.

Other potential customers in Europe were unaware of any deals being struck but refinery representatives were either on their way to Baghdad or making travel plans, expressing satisfaction with the prices set by Baghdad last week.
U.S. traders said they were awaiting U.S. State Department permission to visit Iraq.

U.S. independent refiner Coastal, which lifted about 10 percent of Iraqi exports, or about 225,000 bpd, prior to the Gulf crisis for its refinery on the Caribbean island of Aruba, was expected to be at the front of the queue one clearance was given, traders said.
At current prices, Iraqi exports are expected to total about 550,000 bpd via the Turkish port of Ceyhan and Mina al-Bakr on the Mideast Gulf.
Two experts from the Dutch firm Saybolt arrived in Baghdad on Tuesday to see whether Iraq's oil gauging equipment on the border with Turkey was working properly.
The United Nations on Monday said that Saybolt's inspection was the last step before the oil-for-food deal could be implemented.
